source: Spaniol & Rowland (2023) AI-assisted scenario generation for strategic planning
finding: Early reflections-from-practice paper on ChatGPT for scenarios. AI can make many scenarios cheaply. Their usefulness depends on how well the user draws out good raw material. Authors doubt AI will replace human scenarists.
numbers: No numbers. No experiment. Only the abstract page was read.
limits: Anecdotal, one tool, pre-2024 models. Not a test of the Shell six-step method.
agent_relevance: Use the model as a raw-material generator inside a coded loop, not as the judge of which scenarios matter (guardrail on self-grading).

source: Picavet, Maroni, Sandhu, Desouza (2025) GenAI for scenario generation, state government pilot, Public Administration Review
finding: An Australian state government pilot used an LLM to process policy documents and build scenarios with humans in the loop. Output doubled from 4 to 8 scenarios. Cost and staff time fell.
numbers: 8 scenarios vs 4 traditional. Scenario cost down about 60 percent. Staff hours down 60 to 70 percent. Semantic de-duplication cut manual extraction effort 95.2 percent. Traditional process cited as 12 to 18 months. Number of documents not stated.
limits: Read only the university summary page; the journal page (doi 10.1111/puar.70048) returned HTTP 403. No quality comparison of the scenarios themselves on the page. Self-reported efficiency, no control arm seen.
agent_relevance: Efficiency gains come from extraction and de-duplication steps that code can do. Suggests splitting driver extraction (cheap, model) from scenario selection (program plus human).

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025) An LLM-based Delphi study to predict GenAI evolution
finding: Used LLM agents as Delphi panellists and a facilitator, 5 rounds, to produce structured scenario analysis of the future of generative AI. The same few themes (geopolitical tension, economic disparity) always came out first.
numbers: 12 experiments. Panel of 5 or 15 agents, 5 or 15 responses per agent, 3 repeats per setting. gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 for all agents, temperature 0.7. Round count fixed at 5 (no consensus stop). Geopolitical and the second listed topic appeared in 12 of 12 experiments.
limits: One small model, knowledge cutoff Oct 2023. No human panel for comparison. No accuracy test of the predictions. Authors admit sensitivity to initial conditions was not tested.
agent_relevance: A multi-persona panel with a fixed round budget is a ready pattern for the drivers-and-assumptions step. Persona roles are random samples set in the system prompt.

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025) An LLM-based Delphi study
finding: Authors say bias from the base model can survive prompt-level persona diversity. The order of themes was stable across runs, which may reflect the first questions or the model's own priors.
numbers: Roles randomly sampled (professional background, experience type, field, and more) and placed in the system prompt. Each setting repeated 3 times.
limits: No variance statistic computed in the text read.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts alone do not give independent views (correlated errors). Check output overlap with code, not by asking the model.

source: XFinBench, Zhang, Cao, Liao (2025) Benchmarking LLMs in complex financial problem solving
finding: A benchmark capability named scenario planning (analyse possible financial futures to assess impact on decisions) shows a large gap to graduate-level finance experts.
numbers: 4,235 examples total. Scenario planning: 246 test and 69 validation items, 88.6 percent of them financial calculation tasks. Per-capability accuracy (SP): o1-preview 60.1, o1-mini 50.8, claude-3.5-sonnet 47.2, deepseek-chat 47.1, gpt-4o 46.3, Llama-3.1-405B 39.9, gemini-1.5-pro 37.4, Llama-3.1-8B 22.3. Human experts 75.8. 18 models tested.
limits: This is quantitative finance calculation, not the Shell qualitative method. Name overlap only. Human baseline is 3 finance-master experts on a 1,000-item sample, closed book.
agent_relevance: Do not count this as evidence for Shell-style scenarios. It does show reasoning-tuned models (o1) gain most on structured what-if calculation.

source: XFinBench (2025)
finding: Adding retrieved finance knowledge helped little on future-oriented items. In the oracle setting gains were largest for terminology and limited, even negative for GPT-4o, on future forecasting. The error type over-reliance on supplied knowledge was most common in scenario planning questions.
numbers: Retrieval top-3 with BM25 or Ada embeddings, plus oracle terms. Program-of-Thought lowered most models in financial calculation because of a low code execution rate. o1 overall 67.3 vs human 79.8 (12.5 points short).
limits: Four models in the retrieval analysis. Error analysis by hand on small samples (400 o1 answers).
agent_relevance: Giving more context does not fix forward-looking tasks; the bottleneck is reasoning over branches, which a scaffold must supply.

source: Soru & Marshall (2025) Leveraging log probabilities in language models to forecast future events
finding: A pipeline (trend search, event extraction, exclusivity check, logprob-weighted probability) beat plain GPT-4o on 150 blue-sky forecasts but not superforecasters. Authors frame it as a step toward multi-forecast scenarios.
numbers: 150 forecasts across 15 topics, about 45,000 articles, 240 day horizon, test set 72. Brier: pipeline 0.186, vanilla GPT-4o 0.236, random 0.250, superforecaster average 0.150. Mutually exclusive events checked to sum to 100 percent or less.
limits: Small test set. Human comparison numbers come from other studies, not the same questions. Prompts not published. Stated 19 percent gain over GPT-4o; the table gives about 21.
agent_relevance: Probability bookkeeping across a set of scenarios (sum to 1, exclusivity) is code-checkable and fits a cut-to-2-or-3 step.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: A retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned, ensembled system gets close to, but does not beat, the crowd overall. It wins when the crowd is unsure.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (accuracy 71.5 vs 77.0 percent). Best no-retrieval baseline GPT-4-1106 0.208. When crowd between 0.3 and 0.7: system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. System plus crowd average beat either alone in every setting. Trimmed-mean ensemble.
limits: Hedging near 0.5 hurts when the crowd is confident (Brier worse by 0.04 though accuracy 7 percent higher). Five platforms. Questions after model cutoffs.
agent_relevance: Combine model forecasts with a second independent source by simple averaging; use the model where uncertainty is highest, which is where scenarios matter.

source: Halawi et al. (2024)
finding: Zero-shot and scratchpad prompting alone gave near-chance forecasts for most models. Only the GPT-4 and Claude-2 series beat the 0.25 baseline by more than 0.02.
numbers: 14 LMs. Best baseline 0.208 (GPT-4-1106-Preview). Crowd 0.149.
limits: Prompt candidates chosen on validation set by Brier.
agent_relevance: A bare chain of thought is not a scaffold for foresight; the retrieval and aggregation steps carry the gain.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Dynamic benchmark of 1,000 forecasting questions. Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM. Top LLMs that saw the crowd forecast did best.
numbers: 200-item human subset: superforecasters Brier 0.096, public 0.121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122; best model without crowd info 0.136. Combination questions: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. Gap 0.054 vs a GPT-4o to GPT-4 gap of 0.026. Linear projection: parity when Arena score nears 1406 (95 percent CI 1346 to 1633) or training compute 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28).
limits: Projection from about 10 models, marginal significance (r=-0.67, p=0.046). Combination questions assume independence for humans.
agent_relevance: LLMs do worst when events must be combined, which is the step of combining drivers into a scenario. Code should do joint-probability arithmetic.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd of 925 forecasters on 31 binary questions. Models showed acquiescence bias (mean predictions above 50 percent when outcomes were split evenly).
numbers: 12 models, 31 questions, 925 humans over 3 months. Study 2: showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median raised accuracy 17 to 28 percent; averaging human and machine was better.
limits: Abstract page only; no Brier values on that page.
agent_relevance: Aggregating several models beats one. Watch for a built-in yes bias when asking for the plausibility of each scenario.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Humans using an LLM assistant forecast better, even when the assistant was designed to be overconfident and ignore base rates.
numbers: 991 participants, six questions. Both frontier assistants raised accuracy 24 to 28 percent vs a control that gave no numbers. Excluding one outlier item: 41 percent (superforecasting assistant) and 29 percent (noisy assistant).
limits: Abstract page only; per-arm sample sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Even poor prompts help a human a lot; the loop should measure gains against a no-scaffold control.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Time-R1: Towards comprehensive temporal reasoning in LLMs
finding: A 3B model trained with a three-stage RL curriculum generates future news scenarios (8 themes, 3 items each, diversity filtered to 5 per theme per month) scored for plausibility against real news. It narrowly tops much larger models.
numbers: Average max cosine similarity to real news, Aug 2024 to Feb 2025: Time-R1 48.90 percent, DeepSeek-V3-671B 48.81, Llama-3.1-8B 47.96, Qwen2.5-3B 47.66, DeepSeek-R1-671B 47.46. Gaps under 2 points. 40 scenarios per month.
limits: The metric is embedding similarity to what happened, not a judgement of decision value. Differences are tiny and the table has no error bars.
agent_relevance: Similarity to later news is a cheap, code-computed backtest for scenario sets. Shows scale does not buy foresight.

finding: Authors conclude that large scale or general reasoning alone does not give skill at future event timing or plausible scenario generation.
numbers: Stage 2 event-time score 0.7780 vs DeepSeek-R1 0.7503.
limits: Authors' own interpretation. 3B vs 671B comparison on one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Matches our view: structure around the model matters more than model size for foresight.

source: He & Lim (2026) From control to foresight: simulation as a new paradigm for human-agent collaboration
finding: Perspective paper (CHI 2026 workshop, 5 pages) arguing agents should let users preview simulated future trajectories before approving actions.
numbers: No measured results in the abstract.
limits: Position paper. Only the abstract and opening were read.
agent_relevance: Same idea as scenario planning applied to the agent's own next steps: roll forward 2 to 3 plausible futures before commit.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior
finding: A 25-agent sandbox. Removing memory, planning and reflection lowered believability in order. The full architecture beat human crowdworker role-play.
numbers: 100 Prolific evaluators ranked 5 conditions. TrueSkill mean: full 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, crowdworker 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Full vs prior-work ablation d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001.
limits: Measures believability, not forecasting accuracy. Agents embellished memories.
agent_relevance: Simulating actors is the LLM version of scenario role-play; a reflection step improves coherence.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative agents
finding: Crowdworker condition and the fully ablated baseline did not differ significantly (Dunn post-hoc). Agents sometimes embellished memories.
numbers: Evaluation by 100 evaluators; condition ranks.
limits: Single sandbox of 25 agents.
agent_relevance: Role-played futures can drift from fact; ground each branch against retrieved data.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating language models for human-like diversity
finding: Models produce far less varied answers than humans. This limits how many truly different mini-scenarios a model gives when asked for 7 to 9.
numbers: 20 models. Many leading models gave under 3 distinct answers in 10 queries. Smaller models (Gemma 2-2B, Llama 3.2-1B) were most diverse; larger models in a family often less so. Human baseline: 8 authors per prompt on curated prompts. Paraphrasing and system prompts only marginally helped. In-context regeneration (showing earlier outputs) roughly matched humans; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro surpassed human cumulative utility.
limits: Human baseline is the paper's own authors, a narrow group (they call it a lower bound). Equivalence classifier 79 percent accurate vs human labels. Only Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro were used in the prompting-strategy test, on 100 prompts.
agent_relevance: Generate scenarios one at a time with earlier ones in context and have code cluster for distinctness. Do not just say be creative.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Different models give very similar answers to open questions. Repeated sampling does not give diverse sets.
numbers: Infinity-Chat: 26K queries, 17 subcategories, 31,250 human annotations (25 per item). 25 models, 50 responses on 100 queries: average same-prompt pairwise similarity usually above 0.8 at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0. Min-p decoding: 81 percent of pairs above 0.7, 61.2 percent above 0.8. Cross-model similarity 71 to 82 percent (DeepSeek-V3 and qwen-max 0.82). Random pairs fall in 0.1 to 0.2.
limits: Sentence-embedding similarity is only a proxy. Reward models and LLM judges were also miscalibrated on items where human raters disagree.
agent_relevance: A panel of different models is not an independent panel. Use code to check overlap among scenarios and do not let an LLM judge pick winners.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: The ensemble was statistically not different from the human crowd, and equivalent within medium effect bounds in exploratory tests.
numbers: 12 models vs 925 humans, 31 questions.
limits: Small question count.
agent_relevance: Several independent calls beat one, if the calls really differ (see Hivemind).

source: Soru & Marshall (2025)
finding: Calibration plots show tighter alignment of predicted probability and outcome rate for the pipeline than for vanilla GPT-4o. Topic bias: climate underestimated, energy overestimated.
numbers: Support Vector Regression calibration. Probability variation across runs 1 percent or less at minimum temperature.
limits: No numeric calibration value reported.
agent_relevance: Add a calibration step on probabilities the model assigns to scenarios.

source: Halawi et al. (2024)
finding: The system does better on early retrieval dates and when many articles are retrieved; worse close to resolution and when the crowd is certain.
numbers: Crowd-uncertain subset is 22 percent of forecasts and 43 percent of questions. Platform Brier (ours vs crowd): INFER 0.134 vs 0.104, Polymarket 0.193 vs 0.157, Manifold 0.247 vs 0.310.
limits: Standard errors up to 0.05 on Manifold.
agent_relevance: Scenario value is highest when the future is open; use the operator when uncertainty is high.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Seven baseline prompts included zero-shot, scratchpad, scratchpad plus retrieved news, and freeze values using the crowd forecast.
numbers: Models with the crowd value available were the top performers.
limits: Per-baseline Brier not extracted here beyond the leaderboard.
agent_relevance: Reference-class anchors (crowd value) are the strongest single scaffold element.

source: arXiv listing searches, 2026-11-01: scenario planning + LLM; foresight scenarios + large language models
finding: Searched for work testing LLMs on Shell-style scenario planning. Found none that applies the six-step method and measures the result. Hits were forecasting, finance, software test scenarios and driving scenarios.
numbers: 7 hits for scenario planning + LLM, none Shell-method. Related: SPARC (2602.16671, Feb 2026), a four-stage scenario planning and reasoning pipeline for C unit tests with gains over vanilla prompting on 59 subjects (listing summary only).
limits: Search limits: arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned 429. WebSearch budget ran out after one query. Coverage is incomplete.
agent_relevance: A real gap: our scenario operator would be among the first measured. Plan an in-house test.

source: EcoGym (2026) Evaluating LLMs for long-horizon plan-and-execute in interactive economies
finding: Benchmark of three simulated business environments (Vending, Freelance, Operation), 365 day-loops, over 1000 steps, 11 LLMs. No model leads in all three; models are weak at high-level strategy or at efficient execution.
numbers: 11 models, 3 environments, scored on net worth, income and daily active users.
limits: Seen only via a search-result summary, not opened.
agent_relevance: Strategy quality and execution are separable failures; a scenario step targets the first.

source: Finkenstadt et al. HBR; Iranian sports-business Foresight article; Picavet journal page (search snippets only)
finding: Search snippets list further practitioner pieces on GenAI for scenarios. They claim speed and cost gains with thin methods.
numbers: No figures verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence.
